title: Sampling Distribution and p-Value Simulator
summary: Two groups drawn from the same population, so the true difference is exactly zero. Repeating that builds the sampling distribution, an observed difference is marked on it, and the p-value is shown both as an area under the reference normal and as a count of simulated studies.
learningObjectives: Describe a sampling distribution as the spread of results under repetition when the null model is true.
Read a p-value as a tail area, and as a proportion of simulated studies.
Explain why the two agree, and what that shows about the tail area.
Predict how sample size and population spread change the standard error and the p-value.
State what a p-value is not.
interactionTypes: repeated simulated studies under a true difference of zero
live histogram with both tails shaded from the observed difference
the theoretical area and the simulated count reported side by side
an observed difference that can be moved without discarding the studies
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. The figure marks zero with a labelled line and shades both tail regions, and its description states the settings, how many studies were run, how many landed in the shaded regions, the resulting share and the theoretical area. All three headline figures are text. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Simulated. Both groups are drawn from the same normal population, so the true difference is exactly zero by construction. No real study, sample or dataset is represented.
simulationNotes: Group A and group B are each Normal(0, sigma) with n per group, the statistic is the difference between the group means, the standard error is sigma times the square root of two over n, and the reference distribution is Normal(0, standard error). The population standard deviation is treated as known because the null model states it, which is why the reference is normal rather than t; a real t-test estimates it and pays with heavier tails. Theoretical p is twice one minus Phi of the observed difference over the standard error. Simulated p is the share of simulated null studies at least as far from zero as the observed difference. No threshold is named anywhere, because whether a tail area of a particular size should change anybodys behaviour is a decision rather than a statistical fact.
readmeTopic: p-values as tail areas, and what they are not
